items.title: A precise balance can give entirely wrong masses
items.claim: An electronic balance might read to 0.0001 g — extremely precise. If it has not been calibrated, it might report 5.0732 g when the true mass is 5.0000 g. Precision is not accuracy.
items.prompt: What is the difference between precision and accuracy?

options.text: Precision means repeated measurements agree closely with each other (low random error). Accuracy means measurements agree with the true value (low systematic error). A precise instrument can still be systematically wrong
Precision is about decimal places only
Accuracy depends on temperature, precision does not

items.reveal:
Calibrating a balance with a certified reference mass (e.g. a 5.0000 g class-1 standard) tells you how much to add or subtract from every reading.

Calibrate a pH meter with two buffer standards (typically pH 4.00 and 7.00) before use. Calibrate a thermometer at the ice point (0°C) and boiling point (100°C at 1 atm).

All quantitative chemistry depends on this. An uncalibrated burette, balance or pH meter can give numbers that match each other (precise) and are all wrong (inaccurate). Modern analytical labs include certified reference materials in every batch to catch drift.
items.why: Students conflate precision (consistency) with accuracy (truth). Both matter, and an instrument can be one without the other.

items.title: EDTA can pull rust out of a bridge
items.claim: EDTA is a hexadentate ligand — it wraps around metal ions with six binding sites and stabilises them dramatically against precipitation. Add EDTA to a rusty surface and it pulls iron(III) into solution as a soluble complex.
items.prompt: Why is a chelating ligand so much more effective than six water molecules?

options.text: EDTA forms covalent bonds; water just hydrogen-bonds
Replacing six independent water ligands with one hexadentate EDTA releases six water molecules into bulk solvent — entropy increases dramatically, driving the equilibrium toward the chelate

items.reveal:
Suppose [Fe(H2O)6]3+ + EDTA4- in solution. The product is [Fe(EDTA)]- plus six free water molecules. Even though Fe-O bonds in the EDTA complex are not radically stronger than Fe-O bonds with water, the entropy change is large and positive — one big complex plus six free waters is much more disordered than seven loose particles.

Formation constants for EDTA complexes typically exceed 10 to the 20 — extraordinarily stable.

Applications: EDTA in cleaning products removes iron and calcium stains; in food (E385) it prevents metal-catalysed oxidation; in medicine, it treats lead and mercury poisoning by chelating the toxic metal so the kidneys can excrete it.
items.why: Bond strength is the obvious explanation. Entropy of releasing many small ligands at once is what really stabilises chelates.

items.title: Mercury is the only metal you can pour at room temperature
items.claim: Cadmium melts at 321°C, zinc at 420°C, gold at 1064°C. Mercury melts at -39°C. Sit it in your hand and you watch a metal flow.

options.text: Mercury is not really a metal

Relativistic contraction of mercury's 6s orbital means its outer electrons resist delocalising into the metallic 'sea'; mercury atoms are held together more by weak van der Waals forces than by strong metallic bonding, so the lattice melts at low temperature
Mercury atoms are too heavy to form a solid
Mercury contains hidden noble gas atoms

items.reveal:
Mercury's atomic configuration is [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2. The 6s electrons are relativistically contracted (a consequence of inner electrons moving at relativistic speeds in a high-Z element), making them behave more like a closed shell than typical valence electrons.

Metallic bonding relies on delocalised valence electrons. Mercury's 6s pair is reluctant to delocalise, so Hg-Hg bonds are weak. Calculations suggest that without relativistic effects, mercury would melt around 80°C — much like cadmium.

Mercury thermometers, dental amalgams and gold extraction all depend on this anomalous liquidity.
items.why: Mercury's familiar behaviour is one of the most everyday consequences of special relativity.
